explain.say: Low waves lose very little energy as they travel, so infrasound can cross whole oceans and continents. After Krakatoa erupted in 1883, its pressure wave was recorded going round the Earth several times.

faq.a: Infrasound is sound below about 20 vibrations per second, too low for human hearing. Huge events that move lots of air, like eruptions and storms, make it.
asks: What is sound below hearing called?
What is the opposite of ultrasound?

faq.q: How far did the Krakatoa sound travel?
faq.a: The 1883 Krakatoa eruption was heard as booms nearly 4,800 kilometres away, and its pressure wave was recorded on instruments around the world as it circled the Earth several times.
asks: What was the loudest sound ever?

faq.q: How do scientists listen to volcanoes?
faq.a: They use microbarometers, very sensitive pressure sensors that pick up tiny, slow air pressure changes. Networks of them can tell where an eruption happened and how big it was.

faq.q: Why can infrasound travel so far?
faq.a: The air absorbs very little energy from slow, low-frequency waves, so they fade only gradually. They can also be guided by layers of air high in the atmosphere.
asks: Why does low sound go so far?
Why didn't the volcano sound fade?

faq.a: Storms, ocean waves, earthquakes, avalanches, meteors entering the atmosphere and large animals like elephants and whales all make infrasound.
asks: What natural things make low sounds?

facts: The 1883 eruption of Krakatoa was heard nearly 4,800 kilometres away, and its pressure wave was recorded circling the globe several times.
The pressure wave from the 2022 Hunga Tonga–Hunga Ha'apai eruption was detected travelling around the Earth several times.
The International Monitoring System for nuclear tests includes dozens of infrasound stations that also detect volcanoes and meteors.
